title: Analytic Philosophy in Early Modern India

summaries.example: Imagine making a careful sorting chart for a classroom. You might first name the things you see, then describe a feature that helps you tell them apart, and finally check whether the feature works for every item. Vaiśeṣika philosophers used a similar plan for thinking about everything that exists.
summaries.summary: Early modern Indian philosophers in the Navya-Nyāya tradition developed a very careful way to study reality. Their background included early Nyāya, which focused on logic, knowledge, and debate, and Vaiśeṣika, which focused on what exists. The later school used a precise technical vocabulary and applied its methods to many subjects. A key text, Annambhaṭṭa’s Manual of Reason, explains the Vaiśeṣika system of categories. The method has three parts: enumeration, definition, and examination. First, name the things being studied. Next, give a feature that separates each kind from other kinds. Finally, check whether the feature fits all members of the kind and no outsiders. The system lists seven categories: substance, quality, motion, universal, differentium, inherence, and absence. The first six come from the older list, while absence was added later. Philosophers asked whether these categories had a deeper structure and whether they matched the way words and sentences work. Some proposed divisions between existent and nonexistent things, and between things that contain or are contained by others. The source also explains that definitions could fail by covering too many things or too few. This made classification an active philosophical investigation rather than a simple list.
key_ideas: Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika were older Indian philosophical traditions that later joined to form Navya-Nyāya.
The philosophers used three steps: name things, define them, and test the definitions.
They proposed seven main categories: substance, quality, motion, universal, differentium, inherence, and absence.
A category was connected with the meaning of a word, so language could help reveal how reality is organized.
The categories were not accepted without questions; philosophers examined whether their definitions were too broad or too narrow.
summaries.why_it_matters: This tradition shows that philosophy can work like careful investigation. It asks what exists, how things are related, and how words help us think about them. Its method also teaches a useful habit: do not stop after proposing a definition. Test it for mistakes, missing cases, and extra cases.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical tradition that studies what kinds of things exist and how they fit together.
A later school that joined older Nyāya ideas about knowledge and debate with Vaiśeṣika ideas about what exists.
A named kind of thing in a system for sorting what exists, such as substance, quality, or motion.
A feature used to identify a kind of thing and tell it apart from other kinds.
The act of checking whether a definition really fits all the things it is supposed to describe.
A relation said to connect a thing with a feature that belongs to it, such as a color with an object.

questions_to_think_about: How would you sort everything in a room into a small number of groups?
What makes a definition useful instead of confusing?
Can one feature always identify every member of a group?
Why might philosophers think language gives clues about reality?

summaries.example: Consider the definition “a triangle is a three-sided figure.” It should apply to every triangle and not to squares. The Vaiśeṣika method similarly asks whether a proposed property is both necessary and sufficient for a category. A definition that applies to objects outside the category is too broad; one that misses genuine members is too narrow.
summaries.summary: The entry presents early modern Indian analytic philosophy through the development of Navya-Nyāya. Early Nyāya concentrated on logic, epistemology, and debate, while Vaiśeṣika developed an ontology, a theory of the kinds of things that exist. These traditions eventually merged, and Navya-Nyāya added a highly technical language that was used beyond philosophy, including in poetics, linguistics, and legal theory. The discussion begins with the methodology and ontology presented in Annambhaṭṭa’s Manual of Reason and its commentary. The method, inherited from an earlier Nyāya model, proceeds through enumeration, definition, and examination. Enumeration identifies an object by name. Definition gives a differentiating mark. Examination tests whether the mark is coextensive with the target class. A failed definition may over-cover by including outsiders, under-cover by excluding genuine members, or do both. The goal is therefore close to a necessary-and-sufficient condition, although the account is described as diagnostic rather than essentialist: it need not state what a class is in its deepest nature. Navya-Nyāya recognizes seven categories. The first six—substance, quality, motion, universal, differentium, and inherence—belong to the classical list; absence is a later addition. The category term padārtha is analyzed as the meaning of a word, suggesting a connection between ontology and linguistic structure. Some arguments also infer entities such as space from the explanatory needs of directional language. Philosophers considered whether the list could be reconstructed from more basic principles, such as the distinction between existent and nonexistent things and the relation of inherence. key_ideas: Navya-Nyāya combines Vaiśeṣika metaphysics with Nyāya epistemology and develops an unusually precise analytical vocabulary.
The methodological sequence is enumeration, definition, and examination: naming, differentiating, and testing.
The seven-category ontology includes substance, quality, motion, universal, differentium, inherence, and absence.
A definition is diagnostic rather than necessarily an account of a thing’s hidden essence.
The category list can be interpreted through relations of inherence, but the reconstruction faces difficulties, including circular definitions and the special status of atoms.
The system treats categories as related to linguistic meaning and sometimes supports ontological claims by appealing to features of language.
summaries.why_it_matters: Navya-Nyāya matters because it demonstrates a sustained analytic approach outside the familiar European history of logic. Its philosophers investigated definitions, classification, relations, language, and the standards for a successful explanation. The tradition also illustrates how an apparently simple ontology can generate difficult questions about circularity, primitive relations, and the relation between linguistic practice and metaphysical structure.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical classification of kinds of existent things; in Navya-Nyāya, the list contains seven categories.
The older Indian tradition mainly associated with logic, epistemology, and structured debate.
A philosophical tradition centered especially on ontology, or the study of what exists.
The later “new Nyāya” school formed through the development and combination of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika ideas.
A characteristic that is coextensive with a class: it applies to every member and to no nonmember.
The relation by which one entity is said to reside inseparably in another, such as a universal in its instances.
An entity that differentiates eternal substances, especially atoms of the same kind.
The category added by later thinkers for nonexistence or absence.

questions_to_think_about: Is a definition that helps us identify a thing necessarily a definition of its essence?
Why must a good definition avoid both over-coverage and under-coverage?
Does the connection between words and categories support a theory about reality, or only a theory about language?
Can inherence organize all the categories without additional assumptions?
What would count as evidence that a proposed category is genuinely fundamental?

summaries.example: Suppose a school club defines “member” as “someone wearing a blue badge.” If visitors can also wear blue badges, the rule is too broad. If some real members have no badge, it is too narrow. The Vaiśeṣika method asks similar questions about properties used to define categories: does the property fit all members and exclude everything else?
summaries.summary: The opening discussion of Analytic Philosophy in Early Modern India explains how Navya-Nyāya grew from two older traditions. Nyāya was especially concerned with logic, knowledge, and debate. Vaiśeṣika focused on ontology, the systematic study of what exists. Their later combination produced a school known for exact technical analysis. Its tools were used not only in philosophy but also in fields such as language and legal theory. The entry uses Annambhaṭṭa’s Manual of Reason as a guide to the system. A central method has three stages. Enumeration names each object to be analyzed. Definition supplies a distinguishing feature. Examination tests that feature by using accepted sources of knowledge. A successful defining feature should apply to all members of the class and no outsiders. If it applies too widely, it suffers from over-coverage; if it applies too narrowly, it suffers from under-coverage. This approach is diagnostic: it helps identify things without necessarily revealing an inner essence. Navya-Nyāya lists seven categories of object. Substance is a bearer of qualities; quality and motion are further types of property-like entity; universals are eternal and present in many things; differentia distinguish eternal substances; inherence is an eternal relation; and absence is the later-added category of nonexistence. The entry asks what makes these categories a unified system. One possibility begins with existent and nonexistent things and then uses inherence to divide entities according to how they depend on one another. Yet this reconstruction is not presented as perfect. It struggles with the status of wholes and with the definitions of substance and quality. key_ideas: Early Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika developed in parallel and later combined in Navya-Nyāya.
The school’s method moves from naming, to defining, to checking definitions with accepted means of knowledge.
The seven categories are substance, quality, motion, universal, differentium, inherence, and absence.
The category system is partly connected to language: categories may be what words mean or what linguistic patterns reflect.
Philosophers disagreed about whether the list could be derived from one deeper organizing principle.
The source presents both the strengths and problems of proposed reconstructions, rather than treating the category list as unquestionable.
summaries.why_it_matters: Studying this material broadens our picture of analytic philosophy and shows that precision about definitions, categories, and relations was central in an Indian tradition. It also gives students a model for evaluating philosophical systems: identify their organizing principles, test their definitions, and notice where the system requires further explanation.

important_terms.definition: A system for classifying types of things that exist.
The study of how we know things, including how true beliefs are produced.
A later Indian school that developed older Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika ideas using a very exact technical language.
The step of listing or naming the objects being studied.
A feature that distinguishes one class from other classes.
A mistake in which a definition applies to things outside the intended group.
A mistake in which a definition fails to apply to every member of the intended group.
A relation of inseparable dependence used to explain how features, parts, and universals belong to things.

questions_to_think_about: Can a definition identify a group without explaining its essence?
Why is a definition that is too broad a philosophical problem?
Would a classification based on language necessarily describe reality itself?
What might be gained by treating inherence as a basic relation?
Why might absence be added as a category later than the others?
